name: Markings
summary: Ordinary white markings - the star, stripe, snip, sock and stocking a horse can have without any named white-pattern allele. Held here as one additive dosage locus of made-up alleles: more copies means more white, from a coronet up to a broad blaze and high stockings. In reality the trait is polygenic, with no single gene, causal variant or DNA test: in 1,077 Franches-Montagnes horses (Haase et al. 2013) seven regions explained 54 per cent of the genetic variance in white, KIT and MITF together 26 - MITF about 23 per cent of it on the head, KIT and MC1R (extension) about 10 each on the legs, KIT more so in chestnuts - and the white-adding versions of KIT and MITF add up. The KIT allele W20 was linked to face and total white in Menorca horses. A smaller study elsewhere found other regions and not KIT or MITF, so the picture differs by breed. No genotype predicts which leg or what shape. No known effect on build, speed or the long hair. It runs before every pattern locus, so sabino and splash stack their white on top of it.

phenotypes.name: Wild type
phenotypes.description: No ordinary white - a clean face and four coloured legs, unless a pattern gene puts white somewhere itself.

phenotypes.name: Minimal markings
phenotypes.description: A star, or nothing more than a coronet above a hoof. The commonest thing a horse can have and still be called solid.

phenotypes.name: White markings
phenotypes.description: A star and often a snip, with socks on one or two legs - the ordinary marked riding horse.

phenotypes.name: Bold markings
phenotypes.description: A stripe or a narrow blaze down the face and socks on most legs.

phenotypes.name: Broad markings
phenotypes.description: A wide blaze and high stockings. At this end it is easy to mistake for a minimally expressed sabino or splash, which is exactly the confusion the real-world literature describes.
